visit.ground: A little over 200 acres outside Freshford, farmed organically. Beef cattle on the lower half, sheep, a few pigs, about an acre of market garden with a polytunnel, and an orchard.

hero.alt: The market garden at Skehana Hill, brassicas and sunflowers under a grey August sky

story: Skehana Hill is a little over 200 acres outside Freshford. To the south a hill takes a little of the sun and gives shelter back, with an old hazel wood on its flank at the boundary. Fintan farms it organically, and the cattle have the lower half. The morning Provenance walked it the fog had not lifted, and the herd was lying up in long grass, calm enough that not one of them got up when we walked in among them. That, he says, is what moving them every day does.

The beef is where the farm starts. The cows are a mix of continental crosses and Angus, and the calves are by an Angus bull, because Angus, Hereford and Shorthorn are the breeds that will finish on grass alone. Nothing here gets meal. The cattle go onto a piece of ground for a day, eat what they want and trample the rest, and then that ground is left alone for a long while to recover. In autumn Fintan lets the grass grow tall before they graze it, so they are taking in seed heads and forage as well as leaf, and he will tell you that is where the flavour in the fat comes from. At the bottom of the farm a bog along the river that runs into Freshford holds grass when the rest of the farm has none, and slows the water on its way to the village. The herd spends September down there, fenced well back from the bank, while the fields above build up for winter.

The sheep are finished on grass as far as the year allows, with a little of the farm's own grain in the autumn. A few Saddleback pigs root through a paddock that will be next year's vegetable ground, fed on organic barley, wheat and peas and on windfalls carried up from the orchard, where the apples that drop, and the ones the birds have started on, are by Fintan's reckoning the sweetest. About an acre of beds and a polytunnel grow the vegetables: tomatoes, salads under nets against the blackbirds, kales and broccoli and cauliflower for the winter, courgettes and pumpkins, and a corner every year given over to something that might not work at all. This year it was soybeans and sweet potatoes, and both did. Straw goes on the beds, wood chip on the paths, compost once at the start of the year, and the soil under the straw is the loose, damp kind you can plant with your fingers.

Fintan will not call the farm regenerative. He calls it a journey in that direction, two steps forward and one back, a matter of watching and reacting. He leaves the thistles standing in a field because on a sunny day they are covered in bees, and he is planting native trees in the field under the hill, where the animals will graze between them once they are tall enough. His reasoning is plain: an organic farm has to find its fertility inside its own gate, so in the long run it has no choice but to give back more than it takes. The food, he says, only ever had to be something he was happy to eat himself.

products.name: Beef
products.note: Grass fed and grass finished, no meal. Angus, Hereford and Shorthorn sires on continental cross and Angus cows, chosen to finish on grass. Grazed tall in the autumn for the fat.

products.name: Lamb
products.note: Finished on grass as far as the year allows, with a little of the farm's own barley and wheat in the autumn.

products.name: Pork
products.note: Saddleback pigs, a few at a time, on organic barley, wheat and peas and the orchard windfalls. Last winter's batch ran in the woods.

products.name: Organic vegetables
products.note: About an acre of beds and a polytunnel on a rotation: tomatoes, salads, three kales, purple sprouting broccoli, cauliflower, courgettes, pumpkins, alliums and roots. A corner for experiments, soybeans and sweet potato this year.
